skip_reason: Existing-customer pre-move confirmation call, not a sales/quoting call. Outbound to an already-booked job — 'I was just calling in regards to your move on the eighth of this month' — with the addresses, home size and the 8:30-9:00 arrival window already on file and read back off the record. The rep gathered inventory and access detail and answered FAQs; no quote was delivered, no rate or clock was discussed, and no booking or re-quote occurred because the job was already booked. Grading a confirmation call against the pricing / clock / estimate / Save Your Ass / booking sections would produce a misleading number in either direction (near-zero if scored literally, inflated if those sections were auto-credited as N/A), so it is excluded from the scored set. Note: this is a high-value call type that the current 85-pt scorecard does not cover — see coaching note.
items_missed: The customer flagged a live cancellation risk and the rep left it unmanaged. 'We do have elevators. They're currently broken but I'm hoping there'll be fixed by then. If they're not though I might end up postponing the move.' The rep's entire follow-through was 'I will make that note in here for you' — no check-in date set, no ask that the customer confirm with the building, no alternate date offered or held, and no callback commitment. A booked job four days out was left with a coin-flip on whether it happens at all.

Stair-carry time impact was waved off instead of quantified. On a fifth-floor one-bedroom with a possible five-flight carry the rep said only 'it'll just kind of add a little bit of time to the move but, but it's possible.' No revised hour range, no dollar impact, no crew-size change discussed — so the customer is weighing whether to postpone against no numbers, and the job's estimate on file still reflects working elevators. Direct estimate-accuracy exposure.

Second elevator risk taken in and dropped: 'It's not a freight elevator it's just like a normal passenger elevator. So, there is a possibility that the couch might have problems... and that one like there's no way to reserve.' A three-seater couch that may not fit a passenger elevator, on floor five, with no reservation — the rep answered 'Okay, gotcha' and moved to the next question rather than pricing in the contingency or suggesting the customer lock down building access.

No Save Your Ass prep speech at all — no mention that prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill, no consolidation examples (loose drawer items, photos off walls), no 'take a carload' tip. This is the single best call type for it: a booked move four days out, fifth floor, elevator in doubt, where prep is the one lever that actually shortens the day.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned, which is the natural fit on a confirmation call this close to move day — the email with the mover's photo lands 'a few days before the move,' exactly the window this call sits in.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned even while the rep was confirming the arrival window: 'we do have here an arrival window between 8:30 and nine for you. Does that still work?' The guarantee is what makes that window mean something and it went unsaid.
No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned, including at the two openings the customer handed over — the glass-paned bookshelf and 'dishes and whatnot obviously but those will be wrapped up.'

Fragile-item handling left to the customer's own plan without guidance. On the bookshelf she said 'we'll plan to at least like disassemble in half and we might just take the glass ourselves' and the rep answered 'Okay. With glass. Okay, anything else you can think of?' — no advice on whether to leave the disassembly to the crew, no note that disassembly/reassembly is included, no coverage reassurance.

Box count and packing needs never captured. The rep asked for 'the big items' and for fragile items but never asked how many boxes or whether the customer wanted packing help or materials, despite the customer volunteering that dishes still needed wrapping.
No additional-rooms or additional-stops sweep — garage, storage unit, balcony, patio and any second stop were never asked about on either end.

Customer's name was botched at the open and then never used again. She answered 'This is Theresa'; the rep opened 'Hi Aisha, this is Shany with ein moving' against an account under Risha Nayee, never corrected it, and the customer signed off 'Thanks, Seanny.' Three versions of two names in one call and zero confirmed name use after the greeting.

A clean process question got a hedged answer. 'If I do end up needing to move the date with the elevator is it best to call or just like submit the inquiry contact form online?' The rep replied 'either way is fine... either one of those... Either one is fine.' On the one question tied to the postponement risk she needed to name a single path and a deadline, not offer three.

Agenda opener only partial. The permission ask ('You have some time to just run some details with me?') and the proactive 'do you have any important questions or concerns that I can just answer right off the top for you?' are both good instincts, but there was no roadmap and no timeframe — the customer never heard what the call would cover or how long it would take.
top_strength: Access probing was the best part of this call and genuinely better than most. She worked both ends of the move properly: truck parking at origin ('are there any access issues as far as where the truck will park at the first location?'), the unit number, the fob handoff, then the destination parking on Clyde Lane and its proximity to the front door and elevator. Best moment was pressure-testing the walk distance on the record instead of trusting it — 'is it kinda like a maze once they get like, at the elevator and then off on the floor to kind of get to your particular unit cause I have approximately about a 150 feet' — which surfaced the real answer: the unit is two doors off the elevator, but 'it's more of a maze getting out the parking garage to wherever they'll have to park.' That is exactly the kind of detail that drives a move over estimate, and she found it by checking EMMA's note against the customer rather than reading it back as fact. Her standard-services answer was also clean and confident: asked whether the crew wraps the big furniture, she said 'that's standard for us. So standard services for us is the wrapping padding protecting... there's no additional costs for that. That is what should be happening anyway.' No hedging, no upsell, no confusion.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: when a customer tells you the move might not happen, close the loop before you hang up. Risha said the elevators are broken and she might postpone, and the entire response was 'I will make that note in here for you' — then the call ran another four minutes on inventory and ended with 'have a good weekend.' What she needed to say: 'Risha, let's plan for both so you're not guessing. I'm noting the elevator and I'll flag the crew. If it does end up being a five-flight carry on a one-bedroom, that's roughly two extra hours, so figure closer to $X than the estimate you have — I'd rather tell you that now than on move day. Can you check with your building Friday and reply to the confirmation email either way by Saturday? And if you need to push it, tell me now and I'll hold you a day the following week so you're not starting over.' That single exchange protects the revenue, protects the estimate, and gives the customer the numbers she is currently making the decision without. Second priority: this call sat four days out from move day with a fifth-floor carry in play, which is the highest-value Save Your Ass moment there is, and it was skipped entirely — 'anything small that can go in your car, take a carload; get the loose stuff out of drawers and the photos off the walls, and you'll knock real time off the bill, especially if it's stairs.' Third, and cheap to fix: confirm the name in the first ten seconds. She said 'Theresa,' the account says Risha, the rep said 'Aisha,' and the name was never used again — on a warm call to a booked customer that is free rapport left on the table. Process flag for Amanda, not for Chauny: this is the second Chauny call in the sample set to land as a skip, and both times the reason was that the 85-pt scorecard has no coverage for non-quoting calls (8/25 was a cancellation save, this one is a pre-move confirmation). Confirmation calls are where estimate accuracy is actually won or lost — this call had two elevator variables and a stair contingency that should have re-scoped the job and didn't — so a short confirmation-call mini-rubric (verify details on file, re-scope any changed variable with a revised range, Save Your Ass, Meet Your Mover, set a check-in on any open risk) would put real coaching signal on a call type currently scored as nothing.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and easy to talk to — she answered 'I'm doing great. Thank you for asking,' thanked the customer after nearly every answer, invited questions twice ('any important questions or concerns that I can just answer right off the top for you?' and 'any other questions?'), and the customer stayed comfortable and volunteered detail throughout — though the warmth ran on a loop of 'Okay, perfect, thank you so much for that,' the customer's name was wrong at the open and never used again, and the one worry she voiced about five flights of stairs drew a rambly 'well, I mean, no, not really but, but just know that, I mean, we can do that' rather than a clear empathetic answer.
audio_review_reason: Transcript is garbled in ways that affect the read on both name handling and tone: the customer self-identifies as 'Theresa' while the account and speaker label say Risha Nayee and the rep says 'Aisha,' the rep's own name renders as 'Shany'/'Shanny'/'Seanny,' and several customer lines are mangled ('a force heater like dining table with four chairs,' 'Two coffee table blue,' 'amaze' for 'a maze'). Audio is needed to confirm whether the rep actually used the wrong name and to judge her tone during the broken-elevator/postponement exchange, which is the moment the coaching turns on.
